name: Knappogue Castle
address: Quin, Co. Clare, V95 W8X3, Ireland
architectural_style: Late medieval Irish tower house; 15th-century MacNamara construction with a large rectangular keep and bawn wall; substantially restored and extended in the 18th and 19th centuries; Great Hall interior refurbished in the 1960s–70s by the Andrews family for the medieval banquet programme

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Knappogue Castle is a working medieval banquet venue, not a daytime museum. The castle operates primarily for evening medieval banquets — check Shannon Heritage for current schedule and dates as additional evenings are added seasonally (typically April to October). The castle and grounds are occasionally open for other events. Daytime independent visits are not part of the regular programme.

best_season: April to October — the banquet programme runs April–October; the castle and surrounding Quin countryside are particularly scenic in summer
accessibility: The Great Hall and ground floor are generally accessible. The castle's upper tower floors and exterior grounds involve steps and uneven surfaces.
tagline: Dinner in a 15th-century Great Hall — the medieval banquet tradition that turned an Irish tower house into one of the country's most distinctive evening experiences
highlights: Four-course medieval banquet served in the original 15th-century Great Hall — goblets of mead, period costumes, and live entertainment by the 'Ladies of the Castle'
One of Ireland's best-preserved tower houses — built by the MacNamara clan in 1467, restored with exceptional care from the 1960s by American diplomat Mark Edwin Andrews
Live music, medieval storytelling, and dramatic presentation of Irish history from the Normans to the Tudor conquest
The minstrels' gallery above the Great Hall — restored and used for live performances during the banquet
Located in the Quin–Ennis area of County Clare, at the centre of Ireland's most castle-dense landscape
description:
Knappogue Castle is a 15th-century MacNamara tower house near the village of Quin in County Clare — a region so densely fortified in the medieval period that it is sometimes called the 'castle capital of Ireland.' The castle was built in 1467 by Seán Fionn Mac Con Mara (Sean Fine MacNamara) as the primary residence of one of the most powerful Gaelic clans in Connacht, and changed hands repeatedly over the following centuries: it passed to the O'Briens, to the Cromwellian planter Robert Scott, and through successive owners before being purchased in 1855 by the McNamara family, and then in 1966 by Mark Edwin Andrews, an American diplomat from Texas who had served as Assistant Secretary of the US Navy.

Andrews' restoration of Knappogue is one of the most significant achievements of Irish castle conservation in the 20th century. Over two decades he and his wife Lavone undertook a meticulous reconstruction of the castle's interior — reinstating the Great Hall, restoring the minstrels' gallery, sourcing period furniture and architectural details from demolished Irish houses — transforming what had been a roofless shell into a fully habitable and theatrically credible medieval interior. The medieval banquet programme, which Andrews initiated in 1967, grew from this restoration and has operated — with brief interruptions — for nearly sixty years. It is now managed by Shannon Heritage and ranks among the most unusual evening experiences in Ireland: a four-course dinner served by costumed staff, accompanied by mead, live Celtic music, dramatic readings, and a narrative of Irish history delivered as theatrical performance.
history:
The MacNamara clan who built Knappogue were one of the dominant Gaelic dynasties of Thomond — the ancient territory of County Clare — tracing their descent from the Dál Cais, the same dynastic group that produced Brian Boru, High King of Ireland. At their height in the 15th century the MacNamaras controlled much of east Clare and held Quin Abbey (which they had founded in 1402 on the ruins of a Norman castle) as their principal religious house. Knappogue's tower was designed to the standard Irish tower house pattern of the period: a tall rectangular keep of multiple floors with a substantial bawn wall enclosing a courtyard, positioned to command the surrounding farmland and river crossings.

The castle passed through many hands after the Tudor conquest. It was held by Parliamentary forces during the Cromwellian wars and granted to a Cromwellian officer, Robert Scott, after 1651. The castle's relative good fortune — it was not demolished or stripped of its roof, unlike many Irish castles during this period — allowed it to remain structurally sound through subsequent centuries of declining maintenance. The MacNamara connection was restored symbolically when the castle was briefly purchased by a McNamara family in the Victorian era before its acquisition by Andrews in 1966.
how_to_visit:
**Medieval Banquet (main programme):** The Knappogue Castle medieval banquet is the primary way to visit the castle. Tickets are booked in advance through Shannon Heritage — check shannonheritage.com for current dates and pricing (€80 per person at time of writing). The experience includes a welcome drink of mead in the courtyard on arrival, a four-course dinner in the Great Hall, live Celtic music, and a dramatic presentation of Irish history lasting approximately three hours in total.

**Getting there:** Knappogue Castle is 3 km from Quin village and approximately 12 km from Ennis. There is no public transport direct to the castle — car or taxi from Ennis is necessary. Ennis itself is well connected by bus and train from Limerick, Galway, and Dublin.

**Combining visits:** Quin Abbey (MacNamara foundation, free to visit, 3 km) and the Craggaunowen prehistoric site (a lake-dwelling reconstruction, 8 km) make natural daytime companions to an evening banquet at Knappogue.

faqs.question: Is the medieval banquet suitable for vegetarians?
faqs.answer: Shannon Heritage accommodates vegetarian and other dietary requirements when notified at the time of booking. The standard menu is meat-based (traditional Irish courses), but alternatives are available with advance notice. Contact Shannon Heritage directly when booking to confirm current menu options.

faqs.question: How does the banquet work — is it theatrical or just dinner?
faqs.answer: The Knappogue medieval banquet is genuinely theatrical — probably the most theatrical evening dining experience in Ireland. The format combines a seated four-course dinner with live performance: costumed 'Ladies of the Castle' serve and narrate, musicians play in the minstrels' gallery, and the evening includes dramatic readings from Irish history and poetry. The tone is participatory and entertaining rather than strictly academic. It typically lasts three to three and a half hours.

faqs.question: What other castles are near Knappogue?
faqs.answer: County Clare has an extraordinary concentration of medieval castles. Within 15 km of Knappogue: Quin Abbey and its attached fortification (3 km, free), Bunratty Castle (20 km north — a larger castle with a similar but longer-established medieval banquet programme), and Dysert O'Dea Castle (20 km northwest, with an archaeology trail covering 25 sites). The Burren, 30 km west, contains the Poulnabrone dolmen and Caherconnell cashel — prehistoric stone forts that predate the medieval castles by 4,000 years.
